Q: Calculating time elasped in ChezScheme A:

The MIT Scheme runtime function, which is likely to be the basis for the one mentioned in SICP, is documented as

Returns the amount of process time, in seconds, that has elapsed since Scheme was started. However, it does not include time spent in garbage collection.

A Chez equivalent can be built using the statistics function, which returns a struct with total cpu time and gc cpu time fields (in milliseconds) among others:

(define (runtime)
  (let ((s (statistics)))
    (- (sstats-cpu s) (sstats-gc-cpu s))))

If you don't care about excluding GC time, the function cpu-time can be used instead:

(define (runtime) (cpu-time))

With one of those versions defined, you should be able to then use the code from the book without further changes.

If you do go with Racket instead of Chez, make sure to install the sicp package via the DrRacket package manager (or raco pkg install sicp on the command line) and use #lang sicp to get the dialect of Scheme used by the book.

Q: How can I highlight variables with an any type in TypeScript code in VS Code? A:

Use ESLint with a combination of the following rules:

@typescript-eslint/no-unsafe-assignment

@typescript-eslint/no-unsafe-member-access

You can set them to error or warn based on your preference. Warn will underline the 'any assignment/reference' with yellow in VSCode.

Q: How to use numpy.where on non-broadcastable arrays? A:

You want all of a, b, c, and d to be shape [n, *d.shape]. If you know the number of dimensions of d, say three, then you can broadcast a using a[:,None, None, None] , and likewise for b and c. You don't need to do anything for d since it will automatically broadcast extra dimensions at the start.

If you don't know the number of dimensions of d, you can try:

a2 = a.reshape(-1, *([1] * len(d.shape)))

which uses reshape to add extra dimensions to a.
